# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Voluntary task switching requires individuals to coordinate their actions across
competing tasks. Even under identical experimental conditions, individuals
differ considerably in how they organize their responses. The free concurrent
dual-tasking (FCDT) paradigm provides an experimentally controlled setting for
investigating these differences while allowing participants to develop their own
response strategies. Two task streams remain concurrently visible, and
participants decide which task to perform on each response. Some individuals
predominantly perform long sequences of one task before switching, whereas
others frequently interleave the two tasks. Still others exhibit response
grouping, characterized by closely spaced responses to both tasks following a
longer processing interval. The general aim of our work is to understand why
different observers adopt these different response strategies and which
subjective constraints make their choices sensible courses of action.

Our modeling approach follows the rational analysis program as outlined in the 
project proposal [@bruning2025]. Rational analysis assumes that an observer's choices
can be understood as optimal with respect to a particular representation of the
decision problem and its subjective costs and benefits. For the FCDT paradigm,
relevant objectives include accurate and exhaustive task performance, avoiding 
costly task switches, and maintaining a balance between the two tasks. Given a formal
specification of these objectives, dynamic programming provides algorithmic
means to derive an optimal decision policy. Conversely, observed response
sequences can inform the subjective cost parameters under which such a policy
would be optimal. This inverse dynamic programming
[@kochenderfer2022; @ramachandran2007; @drugowitsch2012] perspective connects
individual response strategies to quantitative hypotheses about their
determinants. To enable scientific inference about these hypothesized
determinants, we adopt the agentic behavioral modeling framework of @ostwald2026.
This framework combines a formal representation of the experimental task, an
agent model of the hypothesized cognitive mechanisms, and a probabilistic data
model linking the agent's decisions to observed behavior. The resulting
likelihood supports parameter estimation and model comparison, allowing
competing accounts of response strategy formation to be evaluated against
empirical data.

In @bruning2025, we provided a preliminary proof of principle through generative
simulations of a simplified FCDT paradigm involving letter and digit
categorization. The agent's reward function combined correct-response rewards
with costs for switching tasks and accumulating task imbalance. Varying the
relative strength of these costs produced qualitatively different response
sequences while preserving accurate classification. High switching costs favored
extended task blocks, whereas lower switching costs yielded increasingly
frequent task alternation, including choice patterns associated with response
grouping. These simulations demonstrated that differences in response
organization could arise from a common optimization architecture with different
subjective cost parameters. 


However, while these simulations provided an encouraging proof of principle for
the rational analysis of FCDT response strategies, their scope remained limited
in both theoretical and empirical respects. The finite-trial task formulation
was solved through a discounted infinite-horizon approximation using policy
iteration, yielding stationary policies that did not account for the approaching
end of an experimental block. This approximation also introduced a preference
for earlier over later rewards without an independently established
psychological justification in the present setting. Computational demands
further restricted the demonstration to four letters and four digits,
simplifying the choice environment relative to the experimental paradigm. The
resulting account thus established the generative plausibility of the proposed
mechanisms, while their explanatory value for individual participants remained
unexamined, as the approach was neither applied to empirical response sequences
nor used to infer participants' subjective cost parameters.

The present report takes a first step toward addressing these limitations by
applying our rational analysis approach to empirical FCDT data from
@bruning2020. We extend the task formulation to accommodate the richer
experimental setting and derive optimal policies by backward induction for a
finite-horizon MDP without reward discounting. This allows decisions to reflect
the remaining response horizon while retaining a computationally tractable
account of task performance. Embedding these policies within the agentic
behavioral modeling framework makes their explanatory value amenable to
statistical evaluation and enables estimation of individual subjective cost
parameters from observed response sequences.

The present report addresses the organization of response choices as a first
step toward a temporal account of FCDT performance. In future work on this
project, we will extend this analysis within a semi-Markov framework, deriving
optimal policies jointly over task responses and waiting times to capture both
what participants choose and when they respond. This extension will relate
response strategies to the experimental deadline and the objective of
maximizing correct-response throughput, while accounting for the contribution
of stimulus preview and preparation of the alternative task to multitasking
efficiency [@bruning2020]. Doing so requires a more explicit representation of
processing time, cognitive effort, and concurrent task preparation within the
agent's subjective costs and benefits. The current focus on response choices
establishes the theoretical and statistical foundation for this subsequent
analysis of the timing and efficiency of task performance.

The [Experimental data](#sec-experimental-data) section reviews the FCDT data
reported by @bruning2020 and describes the PTD-RMC condition analyzed here.
The [Agentic behavioral model](#sec-agentic-behavioral-model) section
specifies the task, agent, and data models used in our analysis, while the
underlying MDP theory is provided in
[Supplement S1](#sec-finite-dynamic-programming). We then describe the
[model estimation and evaluation](#sec-model-estimation-and-evaluation)
procedures. The [Preliminary results](#sec-preliminary-results) section
reports the parameter estimates and model-comparison results. Finally, the
[Outlook](#sec-outlook) summarizes the next steps of the project.

# Experimental data {#sec-experimental-data}

For this report, we developed our approach for a subset of the data reported
in @bruning2020. Using the free concurrent dual-tasking paradigm, the authors
investigated whether competition for perceptual-cognitive and response-related
resources affects how individuals organize their responses to two concurrent
tasks and how efficiently they perform them. Across two experiments, they
examined individual preferences for 'blocking', 'switching', and 'response
grouping' under task combinations that differed in their processing codes and
response modalities. The original data and stimulus materials are publicly
available through the [Open Science Framework](https://osf.io/x6n58/). For the
present work, we converted the behavioral data from Experiment 1 to the Brain
Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) format. For implementational details, please
refer to \mbox{\textit{abm\_preparation.py}}.

Experiment 1 comprised four dual-task combinations, each pairing a
'memory-search' task with a 'classification' task. The local BIDS dataset
contains 49 participant records, whereas the article reports 48 recruited
participants and an analyzed sample of 46 after exclusions
[@bruning2020, p. 1415]. Both component tasks involved either spatial or verbal
stimuli, yielding two combinations with the same processing code and two with
different processing codes. The 'memory-search' tasks required participants to
recognize previously memorized patterns or letter pairs, whereas the
'classification' tasks required judgments about the rotation and reflection of
three-dimensional objects or the parity of digit pairs. All tasks were answered
manually, allowing the authors to vary competition for perceptual-cognitive
resources while holding response modality constant. Experiment 2 extended this
design by introducing vocal responses to the verbal 'memory-search' task. 


### The PTD-RMC-FCDT paradigm  {#sec-the-ptd-rmc-fcdt-paradigm}

Here, we restrict our analysis to the combination of spatial 'memory search' and
spatial 'classification' in Experiment 1. In this combination, participants 
decided whether a displayed pattern matched
one of three previously memorized target patterns and whether two
three-dimensional objects differed by rotation alone or by rotation and
reflection. We refer to these component tasks as *pattern target detection*
(PTD) and *rotation/mirror classification* (RMC), respectively, and to their
combination as PTD-RMC. Participants organized their own task choices, with both
task stimuli continuously visible. Each response immediately advanced the
corresponding task stream, while the stimulus of the other task remained
available for inspection. Responses were made with separate hands, with
task-hand assignment counterbalanced across participants. Data collection
comprised three runs, each containing two 120-second dual-task blocks, and
stimuli were drawn from the respective stimulus sets without immediate
repetition (cf. @fig-fcdt, left).

\clearpage

![Experimental design of the PTD-RMC paradigm. Left: Exemplary trial stimuli
and hand-specific yes/no response mappings. Right: Complete stimulus pools.
Green marks one of the three PTD targets memorized before each
block. For details, please refer to
\mbox{\textit{abm\_figure\_1.py}}.][fcdt]{#fig-fcdt fig-pos="H" width="68%"}

[fcdt]: ../figures/abm_figure_1.pdf

In more detail, the PTD task required participants to memorize three
2D patterns, presented as identical pairs for 15 s before each task block.
Subsequent probes were drawn from a set of 18 patterns, and participants
indicated whether the displayed pair matched one of the memorized targets.
Targets and non-targets each occurred with a probability of 50%. In the RMC
task, four baseline 3D objects yielded eight stimulus pairs, with the right
object depicting either the left object rotated by 50 degrees or its mirror
image rotated by 50 degrees. Both types occurred with a probability of 50%,
so chance accuracy was 0.50 in both tasks [@bruning2020, pp. 1415--1416]
(cf. @fig-fcdt, right).

Regarding task allocation, participants were "instructed to not neglect or
prefer one of the tasks compared to the other" [@bruning2020, p. 1416].
Regarding performance, they were "instructed to maximize their amount of
correct responses in the given time, that is, to perform the tasks according
to an optimum speed-accuracy balance" [@bruning2020, pp. 1416--1417]. No
particular switching strategy was prescribed. At the end of every block,
feedback was displayed for 5 s and reported, separately for each task, the
number of performed trials and the number and percentage of correct responses
[@bruning2020, p. 1417]. Participants thus received information about both
response throughput and accuracy for each task, rather than a single combined
performance score. In addition to a fixed payment or course credit, they
received a monetary bonus for each correctly answered stimulus, which could
amount to EUR 10 in total [@bruning2020, p. 1415]. The article does not specify
the payment per correct response or a numerical penalty for task imbalance
or switching.

In the authors' analyzed
sample of 46 participants, the classification under high resource competition,
which included this task combination, identified approximately 25 'blockers',
15 'switchers', and 6 'response groupers', illustrating the response
strategies described in the Introduction [@bruning2020, Figure 3].
For implementational details, please refer to
\mbox{\textit{abm\_description.py}}.

# Agentic behavioral model {#sec-agentic-behavioral-model}

Following @ostwald2026, we distinguish three components of an agentic
behavioral model: a *task model*, an *agent model*, and a *data model*. The
task model describes the experimental environment by specifying its possible
states, the actions available to participants, and the consequences of those
actions for subsequent states and performance outcomes. It thus provides a
mathematical formulation of the rules governing the experiment. The agent
model describes a computational approach to performing the task and serves as
a hypothesis about the cognitive mechanisms underlying participants' behavior.
It specifies the agent's knowledge of the task, its objectives, and the
processes through which these inform its decisions. The data model connects
this account to observed behavior by embedding the task and agent models
within a statistical framework. This connection enables the estimation of
model parameters and the comparison of competing accounts of task performance.
Together, the three components make explicit the experimental conditions, the
hypothesized cognitive processes, and the assumptions through which these
hypotheses become amenable to empirical evaluation.

## Notation {#sec-notation}

In general, we use time-indexed lower-case letters for discrete-time random
variables and non-indexed lower-case letters for the values they take. On
occasion, a time-indexed lower-case symbol denotes a function. This use is
clear from context and an explicit function definition. Thus, statements such
as $x_t = x$ mean that the random variable $x_t$ takes on the value $x$.
The corresponding upper-case letter denotes the set of values a random
variable can take, with a time index added when this set varies over time.
Collections of random variables are indicated by colon notation, i.e., for
integer indices $0 \le t \le t'$, write
\begin{equation}
x_{t:t'} := (x_t, x_{t+1}, \ldots, x_{t'}).
\end{equation}
A collection with an end index smaller than its start index is empty.
We use $p$ for probability mass functions and overload it for joint,
marginal, and conditional mass functions, as identified by its arguments.
Expectations are used only when the relevant variable is integrable.
Conditional probabilities and conditional expectations given a value are used
only when that value has positive probability, unless a particular version of
the conditional distribution or expectation has been specified (we
understand a *version* as a concrete assignment of a conditional distribution
or expectation to every conditioning value, including zero-probability values
at which the joint distribution does not determine it. Different versions
agree at positive-probability values but may differ at zero-probability values).

To keep probability calculations compact, we suppress explicit assignments of
random variables to their values inside probability expressions and
conditional expectations. Explicit assignments are retained when needed to
specify particular component events, transformed values, or a value denoted
by a distinct summation or maximization variable.

In statements such as "for all $x_t \in X$", the symbol $x_t$ ranges over
values in $X$. This is shorthand for "for all $x \in X$, with $x_t = x$
substituted in the displayed expressions". Such statements include values
with zero probability under the distribution in question whenever the
relevant functions or conditional distributions have been specified at
those values.

When a time-indexed random-variable symbol appears below a summation sign, it
is used as a dummy variable and takes each possible value of the corresponding
random variable in turn. Thus we write, for example,
\begin{equation}
p(x_t)
= \sum_{x' \in X} p(x_{t+1} = x', x_t) =: \sum_{x_{t+1}} p(x_{t+1}, x_t),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}(y_{t+1}|x_t)
= \sum_{y \in Y} y\,p(y_{t+1} = y|x_t)
=: \sum_{y_{t+1}} y_{t+1}p(y_{t+1}|x_t).
\end{equation}
For a function $f$ defined on a set $X$ and a random variable $x_t$ taking
values in $X$, $f(x_t)$ denotes the random variable obtained by applying $f$
to $x_t$. On the event $x_t = x$, this random variable takes the value $f(x)$.
The same convention applies to functions of several random variables.

## Task model {#sec-task-model}

We define the participant- and block-specific task model as
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{T} := \left(J,S,A,R_{\mathcal{T}},p(s_0),p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t),\varrho\right).
\end{equation}
The task-model tuple uses concepts from the theory of Markov decision
processes discussed in S1 (@def-markov-decision-process).

### Time indices {#sec-trial-and-action-index-set}


The trial- and action index set is
\begin{equation}
J := \{0,1,\ldots,n\},
\end{equation}
where $n$ is the observed action count within the fixed time window. It may
vary across participants and blocks but is held constant in each task model.
Actions are selected at stages $t = 0,\ldots,n-1$, and stage $n$ is the
horizon boundary.
Note that $n$ denotes the horizon represented by $T$ in S1. Here, the symbol
$T$ is reserved for the task set $\{1,2\}$, introduced below.
The model conditions on the observed number of responses within a block of
fixed duration. It describes choices over these $n$ decision stages without
modeling the response times that determine how many responses fit into the
available time. The horizon boundary ends the decision sequence without
requiring a special terminal state. The boundary self-loops introduced below
complete the conditional state distribution and do not determine when the
block ends.

### State space $S$ {#sec-state-space}

The state records the two task stimuli, the previously executed task, and the
current task imbalance. We first define these components and then assemble the
complete state space.

*Labeled stimulus sets*  

For $j = 1,2$, let $I_j := \mathbb{N}_{n_j}$, where $\mathbb{N}_m :=
\{1,...,m\}$, denote the unique identifiers of the visual stimuli of Task $j$ as
depicted in Table \ref{tbl-ptd-rmc-stimulus-sets}.

For tasks $j = 1,2$, let
\begin{equation}
\kappa_{j} : I_j \to \{0,1\}, i \mapsto \kappa_{j}(i) 
\end{equation}
denote the participant- and block-specific label function. For Task 1,
$\kappa_{1}$ differs between participants and blocks, as it indicates whether
a visual pattern belonged to the memorized target set or not. For Task 2,
$\kappa_{2}$ is identical across participants and blocks, as it indicates
whether the right object is rotated only or both mirrored and rotated
relative to the left object. Note that to keep the notational complexity at
bay, we leave the participant and block dependence of $\kappa_{j}$, and hence
each task model, implicit. The participant- and block-specific labeled stimulus
sets are then defined as
\begin{equation}
S^j := \left\lbrace \left(\kappa_{j}(i), i\right) | i \in I_j \right\rbrace, 
\end{equation}
such that for $j = 1,2$
\begin{equation}
s^j := \left(s^{j,1}, s^{j,2} \right) \in S^j.
\end{equation}

Here, $s^{j,1} \in \{0,1\}$ denotes the task-relevant binary stimulus label,
$s^{j,2} \in I_j$ denotes the unique visual stimulus identifier, and $s^{j,1} =
\kappa_{j}\left(s^{j,2} \right)$ by definition. Note that including the label
alongside the identifier adds no independent state information. It makes the
task-relevant category explicit for the reward function and the subsequent
agent-model reduction, while the identifier retains the stimulus identity needed
to exclude direct repetitions. Only label-identifier pairs consistent with
$\kappa_{j}$ belong to $S^j$. The label $s^{j,1} = 1$ denotes the task-defined
positive stimulus category, whereas $s^{j,1} = 0$ denotes the complementary
stimulus category. Specifically, label 1 denotes a target in PTD and rotation
only in RMC. Label 0 denotes a non-target in PTD and mirrored-and-rotated
objects in RMC.

Note that because the labeling of the visual stimuli merely induces a partition
of the stimulus identifier sets, the cardinality
of the labeled stimulus space $S^j$ corresponds to the cardinality of the
stimulus identifier set, i.e.,
\begin{equation}
|S^j| = |I_j| = |\mathbb{N}_{n_j}| = n_j \mbox{ for } j = 1,2.
\end{equation}
For later reference, we define the label-specific subsets of $I_j$ and 
their cardinalities as
\begin{equation}
I_{j,l} := \lbrace i \in I_j | \kappa_{j}(i) = l \rbrace \subset I_j \mbox{ for } l \in \{0,1\}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
n_{j,l} := |I_{j,l}| \mbox{ for } l \in \{0,1\} \mbox{ such that } n_{j,0} + n_{j,1} = n_j,
\end{equation}
respectively. Table \ref{tbl-ptd-rmc-stimulus-sets} summarizes the stimulus
counts, identifier sets, category meanings, and label-specific cardinalities.

```{=latex}
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begingroup
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrccl r@{}}
\toprule
Task & $n_j$ & $I_j$ & Label $l$ & Category & $n_{j,l}$ \\
\midrule
PTD & 18 & $\mathbb{N}_{18}$ & 1 & Target               & 3  \\
    &    &                   & 0 & Non-target           & 15 \\
RMC & 8  & $\mathbb{N}_{8}$  & 1 & Rotation only        & 4  \\
```
