# Supplementary information {#sec-supplementary-information}

## S1 Finite dynamic programming {#sec-finite-dynamic-programming}

In these notes, we review the derivation of optimal policies for Markov
decision processes with finite time horizon and finite state, action, and
reward spaces. We make the additional assumption of no terminal states.
We first establish the basic terminology by defining Markov decision
processes, decision functions and policies, and policy-dependent Markov
decision processes. We then establish conditional independence properties
and introduce the return, value function, and action-value function,
together with their recursive relationships. Finally, after defining
optimal value functions and optimal policies, we prove the central result
in @thm-existence-and-construction-of-an-optimal-policy, which shows how a
deterministic Markovian optimal policy can be constructed algorithmically
by backward induction. The material covered here is discussed in @puterman1994 
[Chapters 2 and 4], @bertsekas2005 [Volume I, Chapter 1], @powell2022 [Chapter 14],
@krishnamurthy2025 [Chapter 7], and @rao2022 [Chapters 4 and 5].

### Markov decision processes {#sec-markov-decision-processes}

::: {#def-markov-decision-process}
## Finite-horizon Markov decision process

A discrete-time, finite-horizon, time-homogeneous *Markov decision process*
is a tuple
\begin{equation}
\mbox{MDP}
= \left(J,S,A,R,\mathcal{V},p(s_0),p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t),p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t),\rho\right),
\end{equation}
whose components satisfy the following conditions:

* *Time indices.* For a fixed horizon $T \in \mathbb{N}$,
$J := \{0,1,\ldots,T\}$ is the discrete time-index set. Actions are selected
at the decision stages $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$. Stage $T$ is the horizon
boundary.

* *State space.* $S$ is a finite set of state values.

* *Action set.* $A$ is a nonempty finite set of action values. Every action in
$A$ is available in every state at every decision stage.

* *Reward set.* $R \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a finite set of reward values.
Finiteness of $R$ ensures that every conditional reward expectation below
exists and is finite.

* *Random-variable sequence.*
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{V}
:= (s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,a_1,r_2,s_2,\ldots,a_{T-1},r_T,s_T)
\end{equation}
is a finite sequence of random variables. This sequence describes the
interaction between the agent and the environment. The initial state is
generated according to $p(s_0)$. At each decision stage, after the agent
selects an action, the next reward and state are generated according to the
prescribed transition model. A policy, introduced below, specifies action
selection and thereby determines the joint distribution of the complete
sequence. For every
$t \in J$, $s_t$ takes values in $S$. For every
$t \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$, $a_t$ takes values in $A$, and $r_{t+1}$ takes
values in $R$.

* *Initial-state distribution.* $p(s_0)$ specifies the distribution of
$s_0$ on $S$.

* *State- and action-conditional state-reward probabilities.*
$p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)$ denotes the collection of joint conditional
probabilities for all $t \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$, current states in $S$,
actions in $A$, next states in $S$, and rewards in $R$. For each current
state, action, and time, they specify a probability distribution over the
next reward and next state. These probabilities are prescribed for every
listed current state and action and thereby specify a version even at
conditioning values having probability zero. They satisfy the *conditional
independence property*
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-mdp-state-reward-independence}
p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t}) = p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)
\end{equation}
and *time homogeneity*. Here, corresponding current-state, action,
next-state, and reward variables on both sides are evaluated at identical
values. For all $t,k \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$,
\begin{equation}
p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) = p(r_{k+1},s_{k+1}|s_k,a_k).
\end{equation}

* *State- and action-conditional state probabilities.*
$p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)$ denotes the collection of conditional next-state
probabilities obtained by marginalizing over rewards,
\begin{equation}
p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) = \sum_{r_{t+1}} p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t),
\end{equation}
referred to as *induced state-transition probabilities*. By marginalization,
both the conditional independence property of the state- and
action-conditional state-reward probabilities and their time homogeneity also
apply to the state- and action-conditional state probabilities, i.e.,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-mdp-next-state-independence}
p(s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t}) = p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)
\end{equation}
and, for all $t,k \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$, with the same matching-value
convention,
\begin{equation}
p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) = p(s_{k+1}|s_k,a_k).
\end{equation}

* *Action-conditional reward function.* $\rho$ is defined as
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-mdp-action-reward-function}
\rho : S \times A \to \mathbb{R}, (s,a) \mapsto \rho(s,a)
:= \mathbb{E}(r_{t+1}|s_t = s,a_t = a),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-mdp-action-reward-expectation}
\mathbb{E}(r_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)
= \sum_{r_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+1}} r_{t+1} p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t).
\end{equation}

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

Note that although we use the term *finite-horizon MDP*, the definition imposes
finiteness not only on the time horizon but also on the state, action, and
reward spaces. For an externally supplied action sequence $a_{0:T-1}$, the
initial-state distribution and the state- and action-conditional
state-reward probabilities determine the joint distribution of the state
and reward sequences, which factorizes as
\begin{equation}
p(s_{0:T},r_{1:T}| a_{0:T-1})
= p(s_0)\prod_{t = 0}^{T-1} p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}| s_t,a_t).
\end{equation}
Note that here, conditioning on $a_{0:T-1}$ denotes prescribing the action
sequence externally, rather than conditioning on actions generated by a
state-dependent policy.

The MDP specifies how rewards and states evolve given the selected actions.
We next define decision functions and policies, which specify how these
actions are selected.

::: {#def-policies-and-decision-functions}
## Decision functions and policies

For a finite-horizon Markov decision process, let
$J := \{0,1,\ldots,T\}$, let $S$ be its finite state space, and let $A$ be its
nonempty finite action set. Then the following definitions apply.

* *Histories.* For every $t \in J$, the *history at time $t$* is represented by
\begin{equation}
h_t := (s_0,a_0,s_1,a_1,\ldots,s_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_t).
\end{equation}
We assume that the agent observes states and its own actions, but does not
observe rewards. Past rewards are therefore excluded from its history.
At $t = 0$, the history consists only of
$s_0$.
At a decision stage $t < T$, this is the information available when choosing
action $a_t$. At $t = T$, it is the terminal history. We also write a history
as $(s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})$, grouping its state and action components.

A history is called *admissible* if it has positive probability under at
least one policy, given the initial-state distribution and transition model
of the MDP. For state values in $S$ and action values in $A$, this is
equivalent to
\begin{equation}
p(s_0)\prod_{j = 0}^{t-1} p(s_{j+1}|s_j,a_j) > 0.
\end{equation}
The empty product at $t = 0$ equals one. Let $H_t$ denote the set of these
admissible histories. Admissibility does not require positive probability
under the particular policy being evaluated.

* *Stochastic decision functions.* A stochastic decision function at time
$t$ specifies a probability distribution over $A$ for each history,
\begin{equation}
\pi_t : H_t \times A \to [0,1],
\end{equation}
where $H_t$ denotes the set of admissible histories ending in a state at time $t$.
For every $h \in H_t$, the stochastic decision function satisfies
\begin{equation}
\sum_a \pi_t(h,a) = 1.
\end{equation}
These action probabilities are prescribed for every admissible history.

* *Decision functions.* A decision function at time $t$ selects one action
for each history,
\begin{equation}
d_t : H_t \to A.
\end{equation}

* *Stochastic policies.* A stochastic policy is a sequence of stochastic
decision functions,
\begin{equation}
\pi := (\pi_t)_{t = 0}^{T-1}.
\end{equation}
Thus, $\pi_t$ specifies how an action is selected at one time, whereas
$\pi$ specifies action selection at all decision stages. Together with the
initial-state distribution and the action-conditional transition model,
$\pi$ induces a probability distribution $p^\pi$ for the complete process. By 
construction,
\begin{equation}
p^\pi(a_t|h_t) = \pi_t(h_t,a_t)
\end{equation}
for every $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$, $h_t \in H_t$, and $a_t \in A$.

For a policy $\pi$ and an admissible history, a *continuation expectation*
of a future random variable is evaluated by fixing that history and
generating subsequent actions according to $\pi$ and subsequent rewards
and states according to the MDP transition model. This convention also
applies when the fixed history has probability zero under $\pi$. At
histories of positive probability, it agrees with the ordinary conditional
expectation. Conditional action probabilities at the fixed history are
the probabilities prescribed by the policy there.

* *Deterministic policies.* A deterministic policy is a sequence of decision
functions
\begin{equation}
d := (d_t)_{t = 0}^{T-1}.
\end{equation}
It can equivalently be represented as a stochastic policy whose stochastic
decision functions satisfy
\begin{equation}
\pi_t(h,a)
= \begin{cases}
1 & a = d_t(h),\\
0 & a \neq d_t(h).
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Thus, deterministic policies are special cases of stochastic policies.

* *Markovian and non-Markovian policies.* A stochastic or deterministic
policy is *Markovian* if its time-indexed action-selection rules depend on a
history only through its current state. For a stochastic policy, its
stochastic decision functions can then be represented as
\begin{equation}
\pi_t : S \times A \to [0,1],
\end{equation}
where the same symbol is used for the state-based representation, so that
\begin{equation}
\pi_t(h,a) = \pi_t(s,a)
\end{equation}
whenever the history $h \in H_t$ ends in state $s \in S$.
For a deterministic policy, its decision functions can be represented as
\begin{equation}
d_t : S \to A,
\end{equation}
with $d_t(h) = d_t(s)$ whenever $h$ ends in $s$.

A Markovian policy specifies its action probabilities at all states and
decision stages, including states that end no admissible history. These
probabilities sum to one over $A$ at each state and decision stage. Their
specification is part of the policy and determines its value when starting
from such a state. Likewise, a deterministic Markovian policy specifies an
action at every state and decision stage.

A policy is *non-Markovian*,
or *history-dependent*, if its action selection can differ between histories 
having the same current state at the same time.

* *Stationary and nonstationary Markovian policies.* A Markovian stochastic
policy is *stationary* if, for all $t,l \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$, $s \in S$,
and $a \in A$,
\begin{equation}
\pi_t(s,a) = \pi_l(s,a).
\end{equation}
We then write $\pi(s,a)$ for this common stochastic decision function. A
Markovian deterministic policy is *stationary* if, for all $t,l \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$ 
and $s \in S$,
\begin{equation}
d_t(s) = d_l(s).
\end{equation}
We then write $d(s)$ for the common decision function. Markovian policies
whose time-indexed action-selection rules vary with time are
*nonstationary*.

Note that although the transition model and reward function are time
homogeneous, a finite-horizon policy need not be stationary. Because the
number of remaining decision stages depends on the current time, an
optimal policy may use
different decision functions at different times. Stationary policies
therefore form a special subclass of the policies considered here.
Combining an MDP with a Markovian stochastic policy yields the construct
of a *policy-dependent MDP*, as defined next.

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

::: {#def-policy-dependent-markov-decision-process}
## Finite-horizon policy-dependent Markov decision process

A discrete-time, finite-horizon *policy-dependent Markov decision process*
under $\pi$ is a tuple
\begin{equation}
\mbox{MDP}^{\pi} := \left(
\mbox{MDP}, \pi, \mathcal{V}^{\pi}, p(s_0),
p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t),
p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_t)\right),
\end{equation}
whose components satisfy the following conditions:

* *Markov decision process.* $\mbox{MDP}$ is a finite-horizon,
time-homogeneous Markov decision process as in @def-markov-decision-process.

* *Stochastic policy.* $\pi := (\pi_t)_{t = 0}^{T-1}$ is a Markovian
stochastic policy as defined in @def-policies-and-decision-functions. The
conditional version specified by the policy satisfies
\begin{equation}
\pi_t(s_t,a_t) = p^{\pi}(a_t|s_t)
\end{equation}
for every $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$, $s_t \in S$, and $a_t \in A$.

Note that while the superscript $\pi$ denotes the complete policy, the
conditional action probabilities are determined by the decision function
$\pi_t$ at the respective time. These decision functions may differ across
times. Consequently, even when corresponding state and action variables
are evaluated at identical values,
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(a_t|s_t) = p^{\pi}(a_k|s_k)
\end{equation}
need not hold for $t \neq k$. For a stationary policy, this equality holds
for all decision stages.

* *Policy-dependent random-variable sequence.*
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{V}^{\pi}
:= (s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,a_1,r_2,s_2,\ldots,a_{T-1},r_T,s_T)
\end{equation}
is a finite sequence of random variables on the common probability space
induced by $p(s_0)$, $\pi$, and the action-conditional transition model of
$\mbox{MDP}$. At each decision stage $t$, the agent selects $a_t$ according
to $\pi_t$, after which the environment generates $r_{t+1}$ and $s_{t+1}$.

* *Initial-state distribution.* $p(s_0)$ specifies the distribution of $s_0$ on $S$.

* *Policy-dependent state-conditional state-reward probabilities.* For every
$t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$, the policy-dependent state-conditional state-reward
probabilities are defined as
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t)
:= \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t).
\end{equation}
Because the policy is Markovian and the transition model satisfies the
conditional independence property,
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_{0:t}) = p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t).
\end{equation}

* *Policy-dependent state-conditional state probabilities.* For every
$t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$, the policy-dependent state-conditional state
probabilities are defined as
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_t) := \sum_{r_{t+1}} p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t).
\end{equation}
By marginalization, they satisfy
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_{0:t}) = p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_t).
\end{equation}

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

For a given Markovian stochastic policy $\pi$, the initial-state
distribution, the policy, and the state- and action-conditional state-reward
probabilities determine the joint distribution of the state, action, and
reward sequences. This distribution is parameterized by $\pi$ and
factorizes as
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(s_{0:T},a_{0:T-1},r_{1:T})
= p(s_0)\prod_{t = 0}^{T-1} p^{\pi}(a_t| s_t)\,p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}| s_t,a_t).
\end{equation}

Note that although the underlying MDP is time homogeneous, the
policy-dependent transition probabilities
$p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}| s_t)$ and $p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}| s_t)$ are
generally not time homogeneous. In particular, their definitions combine
the time-homogeneous MDP transition model with the time-indexed action
probabilities $p^{\pi}(a_t| s_t) = \pi_t(s_t,a_t)$. Consequently,
$p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}| s_t)$ and $p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}| s_t)$ may
vary with $t$ whenever the policy is nonstationary. If $\pi$ is stationary,
the time homogeneity of the underlying MDP implies that
$p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}| s_t)$ and $p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}| s_t)$ are
time homogeneous.

In the following theorem, we establish a conditional independence property
of future rewards that allows us to show that the conditional expected
return from time $t+1$ onward depends only on $s_{t+1}$, with no additional
dependence on $s_t$ and $a_t$
(@thm-policy-dependent-conditional-expected-return-independence). This
result in turn supports the recursive relationship between the
action-value function at time $t$ and the value function at time $t+1$
(@thm-policy-dependent-action-value-recursion).

::: {#thm-policy-dependent-reward-conditional-independence}
## Reward conditional independence for a policy-dependent MDP

Let $\pi$ be the Markovian stochastic policy of a policy-dependent MDP. Then, 
for every $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-2$, $k = t+2,t+3,\ldots,T$, and every 
state-action-state combination $(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) \in S \times A \times S$ with
$p^{\pi}(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) > 0$, the reward at time $k$ is conditionally independent
of the state and action at time $t$ given the state at time $t+1$, 
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(r_k|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) = p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1}).
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}

We first prove the stronger identity
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-policy-reward-history-conditional-independence}
p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) = p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1})
\end{equation}
for every positive-probability state-action history $(s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})$.
All sums below involving conditional probabilities are
restricted to conditioning events of positive probability. Omitted events
have zero weight.

To this end, we use induction on
\begin{equation}
d := k-t-1,
\end{equation}
i.e., the number of time steps by which the reward $r_k$ lies beyond
$s_{t+1}$.

*Base case.* Let $d = 1$, so that $k = t+2$. Then we have

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\footnotesize
\begin{align*}
p^{\pi}(r_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) & = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(a_{t+1},r_{t+2},s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})   \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}}
p^{\pi}(r_{t+2},s_{t+2}|a_{t+1},s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})
p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})                                                                                        \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}}
p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})
p^{\pi}(r_{t+2},s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t+1})                                                                              \\
& \overset{(1)}{ = } \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{t+1})p(r_{t+2},s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1})             \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} \pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(r_{t+2},s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1})                            \\
& = p^{\pi}(r_{t+2}|s_{t+1}).
\end{align*}
\endgroup
```

The second equality applies the chain rule. The third equality reorders the
factors and combines the conditioning actions into $a_{0:t+1}$. Equality (1)
applies the Markovian property of $\pi$ and the state- and action-conditional
independence property of the MDP. The subsequent equality uses
$p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{t+1}) = \pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})$.

*Induction step.* Let $d \ge 2$, and assume that the induction hypothesis in
\eqref{eq-policy-reward-history-conditional-independence} holds for every
positive-probability state-action history whose final conditioning state has
distance $d-1$ from the reward. With $s_{t+2}$ as the final conditioning
state and $r_k$ as the reward, the induction hypothesis then takes the form
\begin{equation}
p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{0:t+2},a_{0:t+1}) = p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2}).
\end{equation}
Here, the relevant distance is indeed $d-1$, because
\begin{equation*}
k-(t+1)-1 = k-t-2 = (k-t-1)-1 = d-1.
\end{equation*}
We then have

\begin{footnotesize}
\begin{align}
& p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) \notag                                                                                          \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k,a_{t+1},s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) \notag                                          \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{0:t+2},a_{0:t+1})p^{\pi}(a_{t+1},s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) \notag              \\
& \overset{(2)}{ = } \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})p^{\pi}(a_{t+1},s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) \notag         \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})
p^{\pi}(s_{t+2}|a_{t+1},s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})
p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) \notag                                                                                        \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})
p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})
p^{\pi}(s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t},a_{t+1}) \notag                                                                                \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})
p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})
p^{\pi}(s_{t+2}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t+1}) \notag                                                                                      \\
& \overset{(3)}{ = } \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})p^{\pi}(a_{t+1}|s_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag                \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})
\left(\sum_{s_{0:t}} \sum_{a_{0:t}}
p^{\pi}(s_{0:t},a_{0:t}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1},s_{t+2})\right)
\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag                                                                      \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}}
\left(\sum_{s_{0:t}} \sum_{a_{0:t}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+2})
p^{\pi}(s_{0:t},a_{0:t}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1},s_{t+2})\right)
\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag                                                                      \\
& \overset{(4)}{ = } \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}}
\left(\sum_{s_{0:t}} \sum_{a_{0:t}}
p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{0:t+2},a_{0:t+1})
p^{\pi}(s_{0:t},a_{0:t}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1},s_{t+2})\right)
\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag                                                                      \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}}
\left(\sum_{s_{0:t}} \sum_{a_{0:t}}
p^{\pi}(r_k,s_{0:t},a_{0:t}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1},s_{t+2})\right)
\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag                                                                      \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}}
p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1},a_{t+1},s_{t+2})
\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})p(s_{t+2}|s_{t+1},a_{t+1}) \notag                                                                      \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1},a_{t+1},s_{t+2})p^{\pi}(a_{t+1},s_{t+2}|s_{t+1}) \notag                    \\
& = \sum_{a_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+2}} p^{\pi}(r_k,a_{t+1},s_{t+2}|s_{t+1}) \notag                                                    \\
& = p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1}).
\end{align}
\end{footnotesize}

Here, (2) applies the induction hypothesis, (3) applies the Markovian property of the 
policy and the conditional independence of the next state in the MDP and (4) 
applies the induction hypothesis in the reverse direction. This proves
\eqref{eq-policy-reward-history-conditional-independence} for distance $d$.

It remains to deduce the theorem's assertion from 
\eqref{eq-policy-reward-history-conditional-independence}. To this end, we have
\begin{align}
p^\pi(r_k|s_t, a_t, s_{t+1})
& = \sum_{s_{0:t-1}} \sum_{a_{0:t-1}} p^\pi(r_k, s_{0:t-1}, a_{0:t-1}|s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) \notag                         \\
& = \sum_{s_{0:t-1}} \sum_{a_{0:t-1}} p^\pi(r_k|s_{0:t+1}, a_{0:t})p^\pi(s_{0:t-1}, a_{0:t-1}|s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) \notag \\
& = \sum_{s_{0:t-1}} \sum_{a_{0:t-1}} p^\pi(r_k|s_{t+1})p^\pi(s_{0:t-1}, a_{0:t-1}|s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) \notag            \\
& =  p^\pi(r_k|s_{t+1})\sum_{s_{0:t-1}} \sum_{a_{0:t-1}}p^\pi(s_{0:t-1}, a_{0:t-1}|s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) \notag            \\
& =  p^\pi(r_k|s_{t+1})
\end{align}
At $t = 0$, the preceding state-action history is empty and its conditional probability is one.
:::

### Policy-dependent value and action-value functions {#sec-policy-values}

The fundamental goal of policy optimization is to maximize the expected
cumulative reward over the remaining decision stages, which may comprise
all decision stages when starting at the initial time. In MDP theory,
this objective is formalized through the return, the value function, and
the action-value function. The return is the sum of future rewards,
optionally discounted to give less weight to rewards received later. The
value function gives the expected return when starting from a given state
and following a policy, whereas the action-value function gives the
expected return when additionally prescribing the first action. Together,
these quantities allow us to evaluate policies and compare the actions
available at each state and time.

Their recursive relationships, as stated in
@thm-recursive-property-of-the-policy-dependent-mdp-return,
@thm-policy-dependent-action-value-recursion, and
@thm-policy-dependent-value-action-average, then provide the basis for
dynamic programming and the application of *Bellman's principle of
optimality*: whatever the initial state and first action, the remaining
decisions must form an optimal policy for the state reached and the
decision stages that remain. Accordingly, an optimal action maximizes the
expected immediate reward plus the discounted optimal value of the next
state. For a finite horizon, this principle leads to a backward induction
procedure that constructs an optimal policy by solving the decision
problem at each time in reverse order.

::: {#def-return-of-a-policy-dependent-mdp-at-time-t}
## Return of a policy-dependent MDP at time $t$
Let $0 \le \gamma \le 1$ denote the discount factor.
The *return at time $t$ of a policy-dependent MDP* is defined as the random 
variable
\begin{equation}
g_t := \sum_{k = t+1}^T \gamma^{k-t-1} r_k \mbox{ for } t = 0,1,...,T-1
\mbox{ and }
g_T := 0
\end{equation}

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

$g_t$ thus represents the *discounted cumulative future reward* through the
fixed horizon $T$. For $0 \le t \le T-1$, $\gamma = 0$ is referred to as
*myopic* and entails $g_t = r_{t+1}$, whereas $\gamma = 1$ gives the
undiscounted finite-horizon return. Values $\gamma < 1$ can represent a
preference for earlier rewards or the downweighting of rewards whose future
predictions are more uncertain.

The same return is defined for any history-dependent stochastic policy by
the displayed finite sum. For any such policy $\pi$, the expression
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\end{equation}
denotes its continuation expectation after the specified admissible
history, using the convention in @def-policies-and-decision-functions.
At $t = T$, this expectation equals zero.

A basic but important property of the return is its recursive structure.

::: {#thm-recursive-property-of-the-policy-dependent-mdp-return}
## Recursive property of the policy-dependent MDP return
For $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$,
\begin{equation}
g_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma g_{t+1}.
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}
We have
\begin{align}
g_t & = \sum_{k = t+1}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-1} r_k \notag                  \\
& = r_{t+1} + \sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-1} r_k \notag            \\
& = r_{t+1} + \gamma \sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-(t+1)-1} r_k \notag \\
& = r_{t+1} + \gamma g_{t+1}.
\end{align}

At $t = T-1$, the remaining sum is empty and equals zero, consistently with
$g_T = 0$.

::: 



::: {#def-value-function-of-a-policy-dependent-mdp-at-time-t}
## Value function and action-value function of a policy-dependent MDP at time $t$

For every $t \in J$, the *value function at time $t$ of a policy-dependent MDP*
is defined as
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi} : S \to \mathbb{R}, s \mapsto v_t^{\pi}(s)
:= \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_t = s).
\end{equation}
Here, the expectation is evaluated by starting in state $s_t$ at time $t$
and following $\pi$ from that time onward, using the prescribed MDP
transition model. This specifies $v_t^{\pi}(s_t)$ for every $s_t \in S$,
including states with $p^{\pi}(s_t) = 0$. At $t = T$, the return is
zero, so $v_T^{\pi}(s_T) = 0$ for every $s_T \in S$.

For every $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$, the *action-value function at time $t$ of a
policy-dependent MDP* is defined as
\begin{equation}
q_t^{\pi} : S \times A \to \mathbb{R}, (s,a) \mapsto q_t^{\pi}(s,a)
:= \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_t = s,a_t = a).
\end{equation}
Here, the expectation is evaluated by starting in state $s_t$ at time $t$,
taking action $a_t$, and following $\pi$ from time $t+1$ onward, using the
prescribed MDP transition model. This specifies $q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t)$ for every
$(s_t,a_t) \in S \times A$, including combinations with
$p^{\pi}(s_t,a_t) = 0$.

These constructions specify versions of the conditional expectations in
the displayed definitions. They agree with the ordinary conditional
expectations whenever the conditioning events have positive probability.

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

::: {#thm-policy-dependent-conditional-expected-return-independence}
## Conditional expected return under a Markovian policy

Let $\pi$ be the Markovian stochastic policy of a policy-dependent MDP.
Then, for all $0 \le t \le T-1$ and all state-action-state combinations
$(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) \in S \times A \times S$ with
$p^{\pi}(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) > 0$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{t+1}).
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}

\footnotesize

For $0 \le t \le T-2$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}\left(\sum_{k = (t+1)+1}^{T} \gamma^{k-(t+1)-1}r_k | s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}\right)                           \\
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}\left(\sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-2}r_k | s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}\right)                                   \\
& = \sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-2}\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_k|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})                                                \\
& = \sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-2}\sum_{r_k} r_k p^{\pi}(r_k|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})                                          \\
& \overset{(1)}{ = } \sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-2}\sum_{r_k} r_k p^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1})                                 \\
& = \sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-2}\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_k|s_{t+1})                                                        \\
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}\left(\sum_{k = t+2}^{T} \gamma^{k-t-2}r_k|s_{t+1}\right)                                 \\
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{t+1}).
\end{align*}
Here, (1) applies @thm-policy-dependent-reward-conditional-independence. For 
$t = T-1$, both sides equal zero because $g_T = 0$.

:::



::: {#thm-policy-dependent-action-value-recursion}
## Action-value function at time $t$ and value function at time $t+1$
Let $v_t^\pi$ and $q_t^\pi$ denote the value and action-value functions of a 
policy-dependent MDP. Then, for $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$,

\begin{equation}
q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t) = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)v_{t+1}^{\pi}(s_{t+1})
\text{ for all } s_t \in S,\ a_t \in A.
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}

\footnotesize

We have
\begin{align*}
q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t) 
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_t,a_t)                                                                                          \\
& \overset{(1)}{ = } \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_{t+1} + \gamma g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)                                                    \\
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) + \gamma \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)                                           \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1} p^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)                                                 \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1} \sum_{s_{t+1}} p^{\pi}(g_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)                          \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1} \sum_{s_{t+1}} p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) p^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}) \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1} \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) p^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})       \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1} p^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})       \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})                     \\
& \overset{(2)}{ = } \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{t+1})            \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) v_{t+1}^{\pi}(s_{t+1}).
\end{align*}
Here, (1) follows from @thm-recursive-property-of-the-policy-dependent-mdp-return. 
Conditioning on $a_t$ fixes the first action, so the policy-dependent next-state 
probability equals the state- and action-conditional transition probability of 
the MDP. (2) follows from @thm-policy-dependent-conditional-expected-return-independence.

:::


::: {#thm-policy-dependent-value-action-average}
## Value function at time $t$ and action-value function at time $t$
Let $v_t^\pi$ and $q_t^\pi$ denote the value and action-value functions of a
policy-dependent MDP. Then, for $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$,
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi}(s_t) = \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S.
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}

\footnotesize

We have
\begin{align*}
v_t^{\pi}(s_t)
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_t)                                 \\
& = \sum_{g_t} g_t p^{\pi}(g_t|s_t)                           \\   
& = \sum_{g_t} g_t \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(g_t,a_t|s_t)            \\
& = \sum_{a_t} \sum_{g_t} g_t p^{\pi}(g_t|s_t,a_t)p^{\pi}(a_t|s_t)  \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_t) \sum_{g_t} g_t p^{\pi}(g_t|s_t,a_t) \\
& = \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t) \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_t, a_t)  \\
& = \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t) q_t^{\pi}(s_t, a_t).
\end{align*}

::: 

### Optimal value functions and policies {#sec-optimal-values}

We now turn to the central task of these notes: establishing the existence
of an optimal policy and showing how to construct it. Building on the
value functions and recursive relationships developed above, we first
define optimal value functions and optimal policies. The main result then
shows that backward induction yields a deterministic Markovian policy
that attains the optimal value at every state and time
(@thm-existence-and-construction-of-an-optimal-policy). Finally, we
introduce the optimal action-value function and relate it to the optimal
value function.

Historically, the backward-induction construction in
@thm-existence-and-construction-of-an-optimal-policy traces to Bellman's
finite-stage stochastic recursion (@bellman1954 [Section 4]), with its
finite-state, finite-action form explicitly given in @bellman1957a
[equation (1.1) and Section 2]. Earlier contributions to sequential decision
theory include @arrow1949, whose work provided part of the foundation for
this development.

::: {#def-optimal-value-function-and-policy}
## Optimal value function and optimal policy

Let $\Pi$ denote the set of all Markovian stochastic policies of a
finite-horizon MDP. The *optimal value function at time $t$* is defined as
\begin{equation}
v_t^* : S \to \mathbb{R},\ v_t^*(s_t) := \sup_{\pi \in \Pi} v_t^{\pi}(s_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S \text{ and } t \in J.
\end{equation}
A policy $\pi^* \in \Pi$ is called *optimal* if
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = v_t^*(s_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S \text{ and } t \in J.
\end{equation}
Thus, an optimal policy attains the optimal value simultaneously at every
time and state.

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

The definition of $v_t^*$ does not presuppose the existence of an optimal
policy. Because the reward set and the horizon are finite, and
$0 \le \gamma \le 1$, the possible returns are bounded by a finite constant
independent of the policy and the expected return is therefore bounded
as well. Moreover, $\Pi$ is nonempty because the action set is nonempty.
Consequently, the supremum defining $v_t^*(s_t)$ exists as a finite real
number for all $s_t \in S$ and $t \in J$.

A supremum, however, is an upper bound and need not be attained by an
element of the set over which it is taken. Merely defining $v_t^*(s_t)$
therefore does not establish that there is a policy whose expected return
equals this number. In particular, the definition alone does not justify
replacing the supremum by a maximum.

The following theorem establishes constructively that there is indeed a
policy $\pi^* \in \Pi$ that attains the upper bound
$\sup_{\pi \in \Pi} v_t^\pi(s)$,
i.e., that 
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = \max_{\pi \in \Pi}v_t^\pi(s_t) \mbox{ for all } s_t \in S \mbox{ and } t \in J
\end{equation}
To this end, the theorem defines auxiliary values $\tilde{v}_t$ by backward 
recursion and selects a maximizing action at each time and state. These 
choices determine one deterministic Markovian policy $\pi^*$. The proof then 
shows that this policy attains the computed values and that no Markovian 
stochastic policy has larger values. The substantive conclusion is therefore 
the existence and explicit construction of a single deterministic Markovian 
policy that attains the optimal value at every time and state. The theorem 
additionally establishes that history-dependent stochastic policies cannot 
improve upon the constructed policy after any admissible history.


::: {#thm-existence-and-construction-of-an-optimal-policy}

## Existence and construction of an optimal policy

Let $\Pi$ denote the set of all Markovian stochastic policies of a
finite-horizon MDP.
Then there exists a deterministic Markovian policy
$\pi^* \in \Pi$ such that
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = \max_{\pi \in \Pi} v_t^{\pi}(s_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S \text{ and } t \in J.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\pi^*$ can be constructed by setting
\begin{equation}
\tilde{v}_T(s_T) := 0 \text{ for all } s_T \in S,
\end{equation}
and, for $t = T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$, defining
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-optimal-value-backward-recursion}
\tilde{v}_t(s_t)
:= \max_{a_t \in A} \left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right) \text{ for all } s_t \in S
\end{equation}
and setting
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-optimal-decision-backward-recursion}
d_t^*(s_t)
\in \argmax_{a_t \in A} \left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right) \text{ for all } s_t \in S.
\end{equation}
Then the policy $\pi^* := \left(\pi_t^*\right)_{t = 0}^{T-1}$ defined by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-optimal-policy-decision-rule}
\pi_t^*(s_t,a_t) := 
\begin{cases}
1 & a_t = d_t^*(s_t), \\
0 & a_t \neq d_t^*(s_t),
\end{cases}
\text{ for all } t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1,\ s_t \in S,\ a_t \in A.
\end{equation}
satisfies
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = \tilde{v}_t(s_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S \text{ and } t \in J.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the constructed policy dominates every history-dependent
stochastic policy after every admissible history. Specifically, for any
stochastic policy $\pi$, including a history-dependent one,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \le v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t)
\text{ for all } t \in J,\ (s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \in H_t.
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}

We first note that because $A$ is finite and nonempty, the maximum in
equation \eqref{eq-optimal-value-backward-recursion} is attained and a
maximizing action can be selected in
equation \eqref{eq-optimal-decision-backward-recursion}. We next prove the 
theorem by backward induction. In doing so, we establish, at each time $t$,
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = \tilde{v}_t(s_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S,
\tag{A}\label{eq-optimal-policy-attainment}
\end{equation}
i.e., the expected return when starting from any state at time $t$ and
following the constructed policy $\pi^*$ equals the value computed by the
backward recursion.

Furthermore, we establish
\begin{equation}
v_t^{\pi}(s_t) \le \tilde{v}_t(s_t) \text{ for all } \pi \in \Pi,\ s_t \in S,
\tag{B}\label{eq-optimal-policy-markov-bound}
\end{equation}
i.e., the expected return when starting from any state at time $t$ and
following any Markovian stochastic policy is bounded above by the value
computed by the backward recursion. Once established,
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attainment} and
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-markov-bound}, together with $\pi^* \in \Pi$, imply
\begin{multline}
\label{eq-optimal-policy-attained-maximum}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = \tilde{v}_t(s_t) \ge  v_t^{\pi}(s_t) \mbox{ for all } \pi \in \Pi, s_t \in S, t \in J
\\
\Rightarrow
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) = \max_{\pi \in \Pi} v_t^{\pi}(s_t) = v_t^*(s_t) \text{ for all } s_t \in S \text{ and } t \in J.
\end{multline}
Note that equation \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attained-maximum} explicitly
establishes attainment, which justifies replacing the supremum in the
definition of $v_t^*$ by a maximum.

Finally, for any stochastic policy $\pi$ (including history-dependent policies), 
we establish
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \le \tilde{v}_t(s_t) \text{ for all } (s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \in H_t,
\tag{C}\label{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound}
\end{equation}
i.e., the expected return when continuing from any admissible history under any 
stochastic policy is bounded above by the value computed by the backward recursion 
at the history's final state. The conditional expectations in 
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound} are understood as continuation 
expectations after the specified admissible histories. Terms with zero 
probability weight may be omitted from the sums below. Once established, 
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attainment} and \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound} 
imply, for any stochastic policy $\pi$, including a history-dependent one,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \le v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t)
\text{ for all } t \in J,\ (s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \in H_t.
\end{equation}
It therefore remains to establish (A), (B), and (C) by backward induction.

*Base case.* Let $t = T$. For the constructed policy $\pi^*$, we have
\begin{equation}
v_T^{\pi^*}(s_T)
= \mathbb{E}^{\pi^*}(g_T|s_T) = \mathbb{E}^{\pi^*}(0|s_T) = 0 \text{ for all } s_T \in S.
\end{equation}
Similarly, for any Markovian stochastic policy $\pi \in \Pi$,
\begin{equation}
v_T^{\pi}(s_T)
= \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_T|s_T) = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(0|s_T) = 0 \text{ for all } \pi \in \Pi,\ s_T \in S.
\end{equation}
By the terminal initialization of the backward recursion,
\begin{equation}
\tilde{v}_T(s_T) := 0 \text{ for all } s_T \in S.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
v_T^{\pi^*}(s_T) = \tilde{v}_T(s_T) \text{ for all } s_T \in S,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
v_T^{\pi}(s_T) \le \tilde{v}_T(s_T) \text{ for all } \pi \in \Pi,\ s_T \in S.
\end{equation}
Finally, for any stochastic policy $\pi$, including a history-dependent one,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_T|s_{0:T},a_{0:T-1})
= \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(0|s_{0:T},a_{0:T-1}) = 0 = \tilde{v}_T(s_T) \text{ for all } (s_{0:T},a_{0:T-1}) \in H_T.
\end{equation}
Thus, (A), (B), and (C) hold at time $T$.

*Induction step.* Let $t \in \{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}$, and assume that
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attainment},
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-markov-bound}, and
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound} hold at time $t+1$.

For \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attainment}, the induction hypothesis states
that
\begin{equation}
v_{t+1}^{\pi^*}(s_{t+1}) = \tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1}) \text{ for all } s_{t+1} \in S.
\end{equation}
Then, for all $s_t \in S$, we have
\begin{align*}
v_t^{\pi^*}(s_t) & \overset{(1)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} \pi_t^*(s_t,a_t)q_t^{\pi^*}(s_t,a_t)                               \\
& \overset{(2)}{ = } q_t^{\pi^*}(s_t,d_t^*(s_t))                                                                    \\
& \overset{(3)}{ = } \rho(s_t,d_t^*(s_t)) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,d_t^*(s_t))v_{t+1}^{\pi^*}(s_{t+1}) \\
& \overset{(4)}{ = } \rho(s_t,d_t^*(s_t)) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,d_t^*(s_t))\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})       \\
& \overset{(5)}{ = } \tilde{v}_t(s_t).
\end{align*}
Here, (1) follows from @thm-policy-dependent-value-action-average,
(2) uses the deterministic policy defined by the decision function $d_t^*$
in equation \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-decision-rule}, (3) follows from
@thm-policy-dependent-action-value-recursion, (4) applies induction
hypothesis \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attainment}, and (5) uses the maximizing
choice of $d_t^*$ in equation \eqref{eq-optimal-decision-backward-recursion}
and the definition of $\tilde{v}_t$ in
equation \eqref{eq-optimal-value-backward-recursion}.
This proves \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-attainment} at time $t$.

For \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-markov-bound}, the induction hypothesis states
that
\begin{equation}
v_{t+1}^{\pi}(s_{t+1}) \le \tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1}) \text{ for all } \pi \in \Pi,\ s_{t+1} \in S.
\end{equation}
Then, for all $\pi \in \Pi$ and $s_t \in S$, we have
\begin{align*}
v_t^{\pi}(s_t) & \overset{(1)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t)             \\
& \overset{(2)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)v_{t+1}^{\pi}(s_{t+1})\right) \\
& \overset{(3)}{ \le } \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right)     \\
& \overset{(4)}{ \le } \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)\max_{a \in A}
\left(\rho(s_t,a) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t = a)\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right)   \\
& \overset{(5)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)\tilde{v}_t(s_t)                                   \\
& = \tilde{v}_t(s_t)\sum_{a_t} \pi_t(s_t,a_t)                                                     \\
& = \tilde{v}_t(s_t)\sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_t)                                                       \\
& = \tilde{v}_t(s_t).
\end{align*}
Here, (1) follows from @thm-policy-dependent-value-action-average,
(2) follows from @thm-policy-dependent-action-value-recursion,
(3) applies induction hypothesis \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-markov-bound},
using the nonnegativity of $\gamma$ and the probability weights,
(4) bounds each action-specific expression by its maximum over all actions,
and (5) uses the definition of $\tilde{v}_t$ in
equation \eqref{eq-optimal-value-backward-recursion}. The variable $a$ in
(4) is distinct from the outer summation variable $a_t$. The last equality
holds because the conditional action probabilities sum to one. This proves
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-markov-bound} at time $t$.

For \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound}, the induction hypothesis states
that, for any stochastic policy $\pi$, including a history-dependent one,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})
\le \tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1}) \text{ for all } (s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t}) \in H_{t+1}.
\end{equation}
Fix any such policy $\pi$. Then, for all
$(s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \in H_t$, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) & \overset{(1)}{ = } \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_{t+1}+\gamma g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})                     \\
& = \mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) + \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})                                         \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(r_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t}) + \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                    \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\sum_{r_{t+1}} r_{t+1}p^{\pi}(r_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})
+ \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                    \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\sum_{r_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+1}} r_{t+1}p^{\pi}(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})
+ \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                    \\
& \overset{(2)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\sum_{r_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+1}} r_{t+1}p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})
+ \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                    \\
& \overset{(3)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\sum_{r_{t+1}} \sum_{s_{t+1}} r_{t+1}p(r_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)
+ \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                    \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \left(\mathbb{E}(r_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) + \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)    \\
& \overset{(4)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right) \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}) \left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1}p^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)     \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1}
p^{\pi}(g_{t+1},s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                             \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} \sum_{g_{t+1}} g_{t+1}
p^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                   \\
& = \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p^{\pi}(s_{t+1}|s_{0:t},a_{0:t})
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                          \\
& \overset{(5)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)
\mathbb{E}^{\pi}(g_{t+1}|s_{0:t+1},a_{0:t})\right)                                                                                          \\
& \overset{(6)}{ \le } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})
\left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right)                                                \\
& \overset{(7)}{ \le } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})\max_{a \in A}
\left(\rho(s_t,a) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t = a)\tilde{v}_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right)                                              \\
& \overset{(8)}{ = } \sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})\tilde{v}_t(s_t)                                                              \\
& = \tilde{v}_t(s_t)\sum_{a_t} p^{\pi}(a_t|s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1})                                                                               \\
& = \tilde{v}_t(s_t).
\end{align*}
Here, (1) follows from
@thm-recursive-property-of-the-policy-dependent-mdp-return, whose return
identity also holds for history-dependent policies and (2) uses the
construction of the policy-induced process from the prescribed MDP
transition model: once the history and current action are fixed, the next
reward and state are generated by that model. (3) applies the
conditional independence property of the state-reward probabilities in
equation \eqref{eq-mdp-state-reward-independence} and (4) uses the
definition of $\rho$ in equation \eqref{eq-mdp-action-reward-function}.
(5) uses the prescribed MDP transition model and the conditional independence 
property of the next-state probabilities in equation \eqref{eq-mdp-next-state-independence}. 
The continuation expectation itself remains conditional on the full extended
history. (6) then applies the induction hypothesis
\eqref{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound}, using the nonnegativity of
$\gamma$ and the probability weights. Every successor history contributing
a positive probability weight is admissible, so the induction hypothesis
applies to each such term. (7) bounds each action-specific expression
by its maximum over all actions, and (8) uses the definition of
$\tilde{v}_t$ in equation \eqref{eq-optimal-value-backward-recursion}. The
last equality holds because the conditional action probabilities sum to
one. This proves \eqref{eq-optimal-policy-history-bound} at time $t$.

:::

::: {#def-optimal-action-value-function}
## Optimal action-value function 

Let $\Pi$ denote the set of all Markovian stochastic policies of a
finite-horizon MDP. For $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$, the *optimal action-value
function at time $t$* is defined as
\begin{equation}
q_t^* : S \times A \to \mathbb{R},\ q_t^*(s_t,a_t) := \sup_{\pi \in \Pi} q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t) \text{ for all } (s_t,a_t) \in S \times A.
\end{equation}

\hfill $\bullet$
:::

The optimal action-value function is related to the optimal value function by 
the identities stated in the following theorem.

::: {#thm-optimal-action-value-function-optimal-value-function}
## Optimal action-value function and optimal value function

Let $v_t^*$ and $q_t^*$ denote the optimal value function and the optimal
action-value function of a finite-horizon MDP. Then, for all
$s_t \in S$, $a_t \in A$, and $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-optimal-action-value-function-and-optimal-value-function}
q_t^*(s_t,a_t)
= \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)v_{t+1}^*(s_{t+1})
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
v_t^*(s_t) = \max_{a_t \in A} q_t^*(s_t,a_t).
\end{equation}

\hfill $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.proof}
By definition and with @thm-policy-dependent-action-value-recursion, we have 
\begin{align}
q_t^*(s_t,a_t) 
& = \sup_{\pi \in \Pi} q_t^{\pi}(s_t,a_t) \notag                                                                        \\
& = \sup_{\pi \in \Pi} \left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)v^\pi_{t+1} (s_{t+1})\right) \notag \\
& = \rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)v^*_{t+1} (s_{t+1}).
\end{align}
Here, the last equality follows from
@thm-existence-and-construction-of-an-optimal-policy as every policy
$\pi \in \Pi$ satisfies
$v_{t+1}^{\pi}(s_{t+1}) \le v_{t+1}^*(s_{t+1})$, and the policy $\pi^*$
attains equality simultaneously for all successor states. Since the
discount factor and transition probabilities are nonnegative, this policy
also attains the supremum of the weighted sum. Further, in 
@thm-existence-and-construction-of-an-optimal-policy, we have seen that
\begin{equation}
\tilde{v}_t(s_t) = v^*_t(s_t) \mbox{ for all } s_t \in S \mbox{ and } t \in J. 
\end{equation}
Substitution in equation \eqref{eq-optimal-value-backward-recursion} together
with equation \eqref{eq-optimal-action-value-function-and-optimal-value-function}
thus yields for all $s_t \in S$ and $t = 0,1,\ldots,T-1$
\begin{align}
v^*_t(s_t) & = \max_{a_t \in A} \left(\rho(s_t,a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)v^*_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\right) \notag \\
& = \max_{a_t \in A} q_t^*(s_t,a_t).
\end{align}
:::

\clearpage

## S2 Experimental statistics validation {#sec-statistics-validation}

### Purpose and validation design

The state transition model specifies how a new stimulus is generated after
the participant selects one of the two tasks. Its observable implications can
therefore be examined without fitting an agent model. We used the experimental
PTD-RMC data to estimate the transition frequencies of the stimulus labels and
identifiers, and compared them with the corresponding frequencies obtained
from simulations of the full MDP. The aim was not to reproduce participants'
task-allocation behavior. It was to determine whether the state statistics
generated by the model resemble those implemented in the experiment.

The comparison was restricted to PTD and RMC, which are the two tasks of the
paradigm analyzed in the main text. All 49 participants were included. Their
original run and block structures were retained, as were the task-specific
stimulus catalogues, the participant- and block-specific PTD target sets, the
fixed RMC categories, and the number of trials observed in each block. This
design matching is important because pooled frequencies can otherwise differ
merely because target assignments or block lengths differ between an
experimental and a simulated sample.

For the simulation, actions were generated exclusively by A0. At every trial,
A0 selects uniformly from the four task-response actions. No fitted parameters
and no optimal-policy computations enter this validation. The selected action
determines which stimulus stream is advanced, while the full MDP generates the
successor state according to its transition distribution. This provides a
direct simulation of the model component under examination and is much faster
than generating the same states through A1.

The use of A0 is also conceptually appropriate. Conditional on the selected
task, the transition law for the new label and identifier does not depend on
why that task was selected. Different action policies change how often PTD or
RMC is sampled in a finite block, but they do not change the corresponding
conditional stimulus distribution. With sufficiently many transitions, the
estimated state statistics should therefore not depend on whether actions were
generated by A0, A1, or a participant. Uniform random actions provide balanced
exposure to both streams without importing a behavioral model into the
validation.

The observed and simulated data were processed by the same counting function.
Thus, differences between the two sets of figures cannot arise from using
different definitions, recodings, or normalization procedures. A fixed random
seed makes the simulated comparison reproducible. The simulation remains one
finite realization of the model, so exact numerical equality is neither
expected nor required.

\clearpage

### Transition reconstruction and frequency estimates

Each data row records the state visible before an action. A selected-stream
transition was reconstructed by pairing this state with the next state in the
same participant, run, and block. Transitions were never formed across block
boundaries or across gaps in the trial index. The terminal action of a block
has no recorded successor and consequently contributes no transition. A
missing stimulus in the unselected stream does not exclude an otherwise known
update of the selected stream.

Stimulus labels were recovered from the experimental design rather than from
participants' responses. For PTD, the three targets were read separately for
each participant and block. The remaining 15 patterns received label 0. For
RMC, the four rotation-only stimuli and the four mirrored-and-rotated stimuli
form fixed label classes. Responses were retained when the label-frequency
panels were split into No and Yes actions. They were pooled for the identifier
matrices because the transition law depends on the selected task but not on
the response component of its action.

The upper two panels of each figure show the estimated probability of a
positive successor label conditional on the current identifier and response.
For task $j$ and response $k$, the displayed estimand is
\begin{equation}
\hat{p}\left(
s_{t+1}^{j,1} = 1 |
s_t^{j,2} = i,a_t = a^{j,k}
\right).
\end{equation}
The two successor labels are generated with equal probability by the model.
Accordingly, the bars should fluctuate around $1/2$. Separate No and Yes
panels retain potentially informative finite-sample differences without
interpreting the response as a cause of the next stimulus.

The remaining four panels condition on the current label $o$ and successor
label $l$. Their matrix entries estimate
\begin{equation}
\hat{p}\left(
s_{t+1}^{j,2} = h |
s_{t+1}^{j,1} = l,s_t^{j,1} = o,
s_t^{j,2} = i,a_t \in A^j
\right).
\end{equation}
Rows represent current identifiers and columns represent successor
identifiers. Each observed row is normalized separately. Direct repetitions
of the selected stream's identifier are excluded by the full MDP. Within the
remaining label-specific support, the successor identifier is sampled
uniformly. The matrices therefore display both structural zeros and
approximately equal probabilities over eligible cells.

RMC has a fixed label map, so all four matrices use the original identifiers
1 through 8. The PTD target set varies across blocks. For panels with a target
successor, block-specific identifiers were therefore recoded into three
target ranks followed by 15 non-target ranks before pooling. A tilde marks
these rank coordinates. The same blockwise permutation was applied to the
current and successor identifiers. Hatched rows represent incompatible
conditioning events rather than estimated zero probabilities.

\clearpage

### Simulation comparison and interpretation

The validation simulation reproduced every PTD-RMC block in the experimental
design. Each simulated block used its original stimulus catalogue, PTD target
set, RMC category assignments, and observed number of trials. The initial
state and every successor state were sampled from the full MDP. Only the
action generator was simplified to A0. The resulting simulated cohort has the
same participants and blockwise observation opportunities as the experimental
cohort, apart from the random allocation of actions and the terminal
transition that is unobserved in both data sources.

The comparison is descriptive and focuses on the probability patterns that
are visible in the pooled data. For PTD, the experimental and simulated label
frequencies are both concentrated near $1/2$. The identifier matrices show
the same exclusion of direct repetitions and the same division between
target and non-target supports. The target-successor panels also reproduce
the expected probabilities over the three target ranks after the
block-specific target sets have been aligned. @fig-val-ptd-exp and
@fig-val-ptd-sim show the experimental and simulated PTD results.

The RMC comparison yields the same conclusion. Both data sources preserve the
fixed four-by-four label partition. A label change leaves four eligible
successor identifiers, while retaining the same label leaves three because
the current identifier is excluded. The corresponding probabilities are
therefore concentrated near $1/4$ and $1/3$, respectively. The remaining
variation is consistent with finite counts in the individual conditioning
rows. @fig-val-rmc-exp and @fig-val-rmc-sim show these results.

Agreement in these pooled summaries validates the experimentally relevant
stimulus-generation statistics of the full MDP. It does not by itself test
every conditional independence statement at the level of complete states.
Many fully specified states are sparsely observed, and pooling can conceal
small context-specific discrepancies. It also does not validate A0 as a
behavioral account. A0 is used only to create action-independent exposure to
the transition kernel. Participant behavior and the comparison of A0 with A1
remain separate questions addressed by the agent-model analysis.

The analysis applies the same counting function to observed and simulated
trials. The associated numerical observed-simulated discrepancies are
exported with the validation results. For implementational details, please
refer to \mbox{\textit{abm\_validation.py}}.
